ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A resistor D made of semiconductor material has the relationship graph of its current I changing with the voltage U across its two ends as shown in Figure A. If it is connected in parallel with two standard resistors $R_1、R_2$ and then connected across the two ends of a power supply whose voltage is constantly U, the electric power consumed by the 3 electrical appliances is all P. Now connect them into the circuit shown in Figure B and connect it across the two ends of this power supply. Let the electric powers consumed by resistor D and resistors R1、R2 be respectively $P_D、P_1、P_2$; the relationship among them is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A resistor D made of semiconductor material has the relationship graph of its current I changing with the voltage U across its two ends as shown in Figure A. If it is connected in parallel with two standard resistors $R_1、R_2$ and then connected across the two ends of a power supply whose voltage is constantly U, the electric power consumed by the 3 electrical appliances is all P. Now connect them into the circuit shown in Figure B and connect it across the two ends of this power supply. Let the electric powers consumed by resistor D and resistors $R_1、R_2$ be respectively $P_D、P_1、P_2$. Please write the quantitative relationship satisfied by $P_1$ and $P_2$.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: Figure A is the I-U relationship graph of resistor D, the horizontal axis is U/V, the vertical axis is I/A, the curve starts from the origin O, as the voltage increases the current increases, and the slope gradually becomes larger, showing an upward-curving nonlinear characteristic. In Figure B, resistor D and resistor R2 are connected between the same pair of nodes, therefore D and R2 are in parallel; this parallel part is then connected in series with resistor R1 and connected across the two ends of the power supply with voltage U. Then reason: initially D, R1, and R2 are all connected in parallel across the two ends of the power supply whose voltage is constantly U, and the powers of all three are P. Since R1 and R2 are standard fixed resistors, they both satisfy P=U^2/R, therefore R1=R2=R=U^2/P. For D, when the voltage is U, the power is also P, so I_D(U)=P/U=U/R. In the circuit of Figure B, let the voltage across the two ends of the parallel part of D and R2 be u, then the voltage across the two ends of R1 is U-u. The current in R1 is equal to the total current of the parallel branch, therefore there is (U-u)/R = u/R + I_D(u). From Figure A, it can be known that the I-U curve of D passes through the origin and the slope increases as U increases, so when the voltage takes U/3, there is I_D(U/3)<I_D(U)/3=U/(3R). Therefore when u=U/3, the current of the parallel branch is u/R+I_D(u)<U/(3R)+U/(3R)=2U/(3R), while the current of R1 is (U-U/3)/R=2U/(3R). That is to say, when u=U/3, the current of the parallel branch is less than the current of R1. As u increases, the current of the parallel branch u/R+I_D(u) increases, while the current of R1 (U-u)/R decreases, so at actual equilibrium there must be u>U/3. Since R1 and R2 have the same resistance value, P1/P2=[(U-u)^2/R]/(u^2/R)=((U-u)/u)^2. From u>U/3, it can be obtained that U-u<2u, therefore ((U-u)/u)^2<4, so P1<4P2.
